one_liner: Portable Kokkos SpGEMM (hash-accumulator KKSPGEMM) that beat CUDA 8 cuSPARSE and MKL 18 sparse multiply in 2018 tests.
what_it_does: Kokkos Kernels is the BLAS, sparse BLAS and graph-kernel library of the Kokkos ecosystem; this entry is its sparse matrix-matrix multiply. You call KokkosSparse::spgemm_symbolic then spgemm_numeric with a KokkosKernelsHandle on KokkosSparse::CrsMatrix objects (or the one-shot KokkosSparse::spgemm(A, B)), so it is not an API drop-in for cuSPARSE or mkl_sparse_sp2m. The symbolic phase computes C's structure once and the numeric phase can be rerun when only the values change.
how_it_is_fast: Row-wise (Gustavson) two-phase SpGEMM. The symbolic phase compresses B's column indices into bit sets so structure counting touches fewer words. The numeric phase accumulates each output row in a two-level hash map: level 1 in team scratch (GPU shared) memory, level 2 in chunks from a pre-allocated uniform memory pool in global memory. On CPUs it switches to dense accumulators when the problem looks dense. Team and vector sizes are chosen from a flop estimate per row, and one templated source covers the CPU and GPU backends (the Deveci et al. 'Multi-threaded Sparse Matrix-Matrix Multiplication for Many-Core and GPU Architectures' design).
when_to_use: You need one SpGEMM code path across OpenMP CPUs and NVIDIA, AMD (HIP) or Intel (SYCL) GPUs instead of maintaining cuSPARSE, rocSPARSE and MKL calls separately.
Repeated products with fixed sparsity and changing values, such as algebraic multigrid setup (A*P, R*AP): run symbolic once and reuse the handle for numeric.
Your code already uses Kokkos or Trilinos (Tpetra builds on Kokkos Kernels), so the dependency is already paid for.
Many-core CPUs where vendor sparse-sparse multiply is weak: in the 2018 KNL runs it beat MKL 18's two-phase variants by 1.8-3.75x geomean.
You also want the graph kernels that share the machinery (graph coloring, triangle counting, Gauss-Seidel with coloring).
when_not_to_use: Peak CUDA-only SpGEMM throughput: the repo's own 2018 P100 tables put Nsparse ahead (KKSPGEMM 0.92x geomean, faster on 28 of 77), and the spECK paper (PPoPP '20, search snippet only) found KokkosKernels best on 3 of 2,263 matrices, at 2730% of the best method's time on average; GPU-specific codes like spECK or OpSparse are faster.
You need current numbers: the only published comparison is from 2018 (CUDA 8 cuSPARSE, MKL 18.0, P100, KNL), and today's perf_test driver no longer runs the vendor baselines.
Small or one-off products in a code without Kokkos: you must build Kokkos plus Kokkos Kernels with explicit template instantiation, which takes a long time and now requires C++20.
Distributed-memory SpGEMM: the kernels are local to one process; MPI distribution has to come from a layer such as Tpetra.

Very large graphs on some CPU backends: issue #2291 reports a numeric-phase segfault on uk-2005 (39.5M rows, OpenMP, aarch64), and issue #1542 (open) reports openmp.sparse_spgemm hanging with GCC 10 and ARMPL 21.

integration.form: static or shared lib (CMake or Spack), with explicit template instantiation (ETI) for the scalar, ordinal, offset and device types chosen at configure time
integration.dependencies: Kokkos core (current develop requires Kokkos 5.1.1+); optional TPLs cuSPARSE, rocSPARSE, MKL, cuBLAS, BLAS/LAPACK, MAGMA
integration.min_toolchain: C++20, inherited from Kokkos 5 (Kokkos changelog: GCC 10.4+ for C++20; CMake 3.25.2 for CUDA C++20); Kokkos Kernels' own CMake minimum is 3.16
integration.platforms: any Kokkos backend: Serial, OpenMP, Threads, CUDA, HIP, SYCL; x86-64, aarch64, Power, NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs
integration.thread_safety: not documented for SpGEMM; each handle holds state for one A*B sparsity pattern

gotchas: The handle's default SPGEMM_DEFAULT dispatches to the vendor TPL (cuSPARSE on CUDA, rocSPARSE on HIP, MKL) when that TPL is enabled at build time, so the default path can be the baseline itself. Request SPGEMM_KK to get the native kernel that was benchmarked; the README says KKMEM is outdated and KKSPGEMM is the default native algorithm. Issue #3153 (closed July 2026) was a regression in this routing.
A handle cannot be reused for a product with a different sparsity pattern; spgemm_symbolic throws if the rowptrs or entries of A or B differ from the first call.
On GPUs the level-2 hash pool is capped at half of the free device memory and rounded down to a power-of-two number of chunks, so on a nearly full device teams share chunks and contend.

Correctness reports exist on less-tested backends: wrong entries with HIP at -O0 on MI50 (#2083, closed), a hang on tiny matrices with SYCL (#1668, open), and a float unit-test failure on serial and OpenMP (#2232, closed).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Kokkos Kernels over spECK, OpSparse or TileSpGEMM when you need a maintained, vendor-portable library that also runs on CPUs and AMD or Intel GPUs and supports symbolic reuse. Pick those CUDA-only research codes when raw NVIDIA SpGEMM speed is the only goal; their papers report wins over cuSPARSE and nsparse, which Kokkos Kernels does not beat.
verified_claims_summary: 2018 wiki data (Kokkos 2.50 / Kokkos Kernels 2.60, symbolic plus numeric, 81-83 SuiteSparse products, best time over thread counts). On a Tesla P100 with CUDA 8.0.44 and gcc 5.4, KKSPGEMM beat cuSPARSE by a 3.61x geomean (faster on 75 of 81) but lost to Nsparse (0.92x). On 68-core KNL with icpc and MKL 18.0.128 it beat MKL by 1.19-1.25x (inspector-executor) and 1.79-3.75x (two-phase variants), and on Power8 it beat ViennaCL OpenMP by 2.79x; all ratios were derived from the linked xlsx tables.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-10-01; release 5.2.0, which needs Kokkos 5.1.1+), Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, 403 stars, used under Trilinos; the SpGEMM benchmark wiki is deprecated and reproducing it needs the 2.6.00-era tag.
